h1: Texas HOA Selective Enforcement Challenge Letter
metaTitle: Texas HOA Selective Enforcement Demand Letter Tool
metaDescription: Generate a Texas HOA selective enforcement challenge demand letter. Cite Chapter 209 protections, demand fair treatment, and stop discriminatory rule enforcement fast.
statuteCitation: Texas Property Code Chapter 209 (Texas Residential Property Owners Protection Act) and Tex. Prop. Code § 202.004
deadline: 30 days to cure violation after written notice
penalty: Court-assessed civil damages up to $200 per day of violation (§ 202.004(c)); reasonable attorney's fees to a prevailing party who asserted the action (§ 5.006)
introParagraph: If your Texas HOA is fining you for something your neighbors get away with, you may have a selective enforcement claim. Texas law requires homeowner associations to enforce their deed restrictions consistently and in good faith. When a board singles out one homeowner while ignoring identical violations next door, that uneven treatment can be challenged under the Texas Residential Property Owners Protection Act and long-standing Texas case law. A well-drafted demand letter often resolves the dispute before it reaches court, forcing the HOA to either drop the fine, apply the rule fairly to everyone, or face civil damages. This page explains how Texas selective enforcement law works and how a demand letter can protect your rights.
lawExplanation:
Texas law governing HOAs is found primarily in Chapters 202 and 209 of the Texas Property Code. Section 202.004(a) provides that an association's exercise of discretionary authority concerning a restrictive covenant is presumed reasonable unless the court determines by a preponderance of the evidence that it was arbitrary, capricious, or discriminatory. Texas courts have repeatedly held that selective enforcement is a valid affirmative defense and a basis for affirmative claims. That presumption does not protect enforcement that is arbitrary, capricious, or discriminatory, so evidence that the HOA knowingly tolerated the same conduct by others is relevant to rebutting it.

To prove selective enforcement in Texas, a homeowner generally must show: (1) the HOA had knowledge of similar violations by other owners; (2) the HOA failed to enforce against those owners; and (3) the HOA singled out the homeowner without a rational basis. Photographs, dated records, neighbor statements, and prior board correspondence are powerful evidence.

Chapter 209 adds further protections. Before an HOA may fine, suspend privileges, or pursue judicial foreclosure, it must send written notice describing the violation, providing a reasonable opportunity to cure (at least 30 days for most violations under § 209.006), and informing the owner of the right to a hearing before the board under § 209.007. If the HOA skips these steps or applies them unevenly, the enforcement action is vulnerable. Section 202.004(c) allows a court to assess civil damages for the violation of a restrictive covenant of up to $200 for each day of the violation.
letterStrategy: A Texas selective enforcement demand letter works because Chapter 209's notice-and-hearing rules and § 202.004 give an owner legal grounds to push back when enforcement is arbitrary, capricious, or discriminatory. Your letter should do five things. First, identify the specific restriction the HOA claims you violated and quote the exact deed restriction or rule. Second, document comparable violations by other homeowners that the board has ignored—addresses, dates, photographs, and any prior complaints you submitted are critical. Third, cite the controlling law: § 202.004(a)'s presumption of reasonableness (which does not cover arbitrary, capricious, or discriminatory enforcement) and Chapter 209's notice and hearing procedures. Fourth, demand specific relief: withdrawal of the violation notice, reversal of any fines or attorney's fees charged to your account, and written confirmation that the matter is closed. Fifth, set a firm deadline—typically 14 to 30 days—and warn that continued enforcement will trigger a request for a § 209.007 hearing and potential litigation seeking civil damages under § 202.004(c) and attorney's fees where § 5.006 allows. Send the letter by certified mail, return receipt requested, to the HOA's management company and the registered agent listed with the Texas Secretary of State or county records. Keep copies of everything. A clear, statute-grounded letter shifts leverage immediately because the board's lawyer will recognize the litigation risk and usually recommend resolution.
proceduralNotes: If the HOA refuses to back down, Texas homeowners can request a board hearing under § 209.007 within 30 days of the notice. Litigation can be filed in justice court (small claims) for matters up to $20,000, including attorney's fees, or in district court for larger claims or injunctive relief. Justice court filing fees in Texas typically run $54–$100 depending on county. Statutes of limitation vary, but an action with no specific limitations period generally must be brought within four years (Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code § 16.051). A prevailing party who asserted an action for breach of a restrictive covenant is entitled to reasonable attorney's fees under § 5.006 of the Property Code, so weigh the litigation risk. Mediation is required for many HOA disputes under § 209.0051.

faq.q: What counts as selective enforcement by a Texas HOA?
faq.a: Selective enforcement happens when an HOA enforces a deed restriction or rule against you while knowingly ignoring identical or similar violations by other owners. Examples include fining you for a fence color while neighbors have the same color, citing your RV while three others sit on driveways unchallenged, or enforcing a landscaping rule only after a personal dispute with a board member. Under Texas Property Code § 202.004(a), an association's discretionary enforcement is presumed reasonable unless a court finds it arbitrary, capricious, or discriminatory. Documented patterns of inconsistent enforcement are the foundation of a successful challenge.

faq.q: How much time does my HOA have to give me to fix the violation?
faq.a: Under Texas Property Code § 209.006, the HOA must send written notice describing the violation and provide a reasonable period to cure—generally at least 30 days for most curable violations. The notice must also explain your right to request a hearing before the board under § 209.007. If the HOA imposes fines, suspends privileges, or files suit without giving proper notice and cure time, the enforcement action can be invalidated regardless of whether you actually violated the rule.

faq.q: Can I recover attorney's fees if I sue my Texas HOA?
faq.a: Yes, in some cases. Under Texas Property Code § 5.006, in an action based on breach of a restrictive covenant the court shall allow a prevailing party who asserted the action reasonable attorney's fees. Section 202.004(c) also allows civil damages up to $200 per day of violation. However, fee-shifting works both ways—if you lose, the HOA can collect its fees from you. That is why a strong demand letter and well-documented evidence of selective enforcement are essential before filing. Many disputes settle once the HOA's lawyer reviews the exposure.

faq.q: Do I have to go to mediation before filing suit?
faq.a: Often, yes. Texas Property Code § 209.0051 and many HOA governing documents require alternative dispute resolution or mediation before litigation over enforcement matters. Some associations also require an internal hearing under § 209.007 first. Skipping required ADR can get your case dismissed or delayed. A demand letter is a smart first step because it satisfies good-faith negotiation expectations, creates a paper trail, and frequently resolves the dispute without the cost of mediation or court.

faq.q: Where do I file if the HOA won't back down?
faq.a: For claims up to $20,000—including most fine reversals and damages—you can file in your local Texas justice court (small claims). Larger claims, injunctions to stop enforcement, or foreclosure defense usually belong in county or district court. Filing fees in justice court generally range from $54 to $100. You'll need to serve the HOA through its registered agent. Bring your demand letter, certified mail receipt, photos of comparable violations, and the HOA's governing documents to support your selective enforcement claim.
